ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Confucius, the classical teacher whom Chan masters quote, compare with case figures, praise, and deliberately cut down.
EvidenceBody: The record does not deploy him only as a foil. One transmission account quotes his “silently know it” and “one thread runs through it,” then explicitly says that these sayings accord with the subtle purport of the lineage. Another biography says the moment when Longtan met Tianhuang secretly accords with Confucius's statement “Do you think I conceal something? I conceal nothing from you,” making his sentence a comparator for a Chan encounter. Dahui places him beside the buddha and Laozi: after not doubting any of the three, one should borrow their nostrils and breathe out oneself. A later letter pairs Śākyamuni's flower-holding hand with Confucius's lute-playing hand as instances of the same human use of a hand. The same corpus also handles him sharply. One address says, “Confucius did not recognize written characters; Bodhidharma did not understand Chan,” while Juelang's verse says Confucius once displayed the first mechanism. Yongjue makes him hear a hall display and fall over laughing, and a recorded emperor-master exchange openly ranks Confucius, Mencius, and Laozi. An entire section titled Confucius's Staff says people know the lineage uses the staff but do not know that Confucius was skilled in using it; his sayings become blows that draw blood without leaving a mark, and the dead-letter Confucius is finally said to wield a living staff. The Zen deviation is this public re-siting: Confucius's sayings and gestures are compared directly with Chan encounters and buddha cases, while the figure can be affirmed, borrowed from, ranked, struck through staff language, or deflated without being protected as a remote authority.
